moleCalc.title: Mole Calculator
moleCalc.description: Convert between mass m and amount n using molar mass M: n = m/M and m = nM. For gas conversions this calculator assumes an ideal gas at 0 °C and 100 kPa, with Vₘ ≈ 22.7 dm³/mol. The mole counts specified particles; it is not a unit of mass.
moleCalc.stpNote: The gas conversion uses the ideal-gas approximation Vₘ ≈ 22.7 dm³/mol at 0 °C and 100 kPa. Other temperatures, pressures and real gases require appropriate values.
moleCalc.invalidInput: Enter a finite non-negative amount, mass or volume, and a positive molar mass for mass conversions.

energyProfile.title: Energy Profile Diagram
energyProfile.description: Compare reactant and product enthalpy levels along an illustrative reaction coordinate. ΔH is product minus reactant level; the forward activation barrier is the rise from reactants to the peak. The peak stays above both endpoints. The horizontal axis is reaction progress, not time.
energyProfile.exoSummary: products end up at lower energy than reactants. Heat is released. ΔH is negative.
energyProfile.endoSummary: products end up at higher energy than reactants. Heat is absorbed. ΔH is positive.
energyProfile.catalystNote: A catalyst would lower the peak (smaller E_a) without changing the start or end positions — ΔH stays the same.

contrast.en: Breaking bonds requires energy; making bonds releases it. Overall heat change depends on both contributions.
contrast.ru: Разрыв связей требует энергии, образование связей выделяет её. Общий тепловой эффект зависит от обоих вкладов.

atmosphere.intro: From the early atmosphere through to climate change. Topic 4 in the teacher's revision booklet.

history.title: History of the atmosphere
history.body: Earth's atmosphere has changed through outgassing, ocean formation, rock reactions and life. Oxygen-producing photosynthesis preceded the major atmospheric oxygen rise about 2.4 billion years ago. Dry air today is approximately 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen and 0.9% argon; CO₂ is a smaller, changing component.

carbonRocks.title: Carbon locked in rocks
carbonRocks.body: Carbon is stored in carbonate rocks and in organic deposits such as fossil fuels. Many marine organisms build calcium carbonate structures that can contribute to sedimentary rocks after burial. Chemical precipitation also forms carbonates; fossil fuels form from buried organic matter through different processes.

greenhouse.title: Greenhouse effect
greenhouse.body: The greenhouse effect is warming associated with gases that absorb and emit infrared radiation. The surface absorbs sunlight and emits infrared energy; greenhouse gases reduce the rate at which this energy escapes to space. The natural effect sustains warmer conditions, and increased greenhouse-gas concentrations alter Earth's energy balance.

items.cause: Human-driven climate change results chiefly from increased greenhouse-gas concentrations caused by fossil-fuel use, land-use change and other activities. CO₂, methane and nitrous oxide differ in lifetime and warming effect. A comparison such as methane's relative warming requires a stated time horizon and metric.
items.evidence: Evidence of climate change comes from long-term measurements of temperature, ocean heat, sea level, ice and ecological responses. Attribution uses observations and physical models to test possible causes. One unusual weather event alone does not define a climate trend.
items.consequences: Climate change alters risks to ecosystems and societies through heat, changing rainfall, sea-level rise and other effects. Impacts vary by region and vulnerability. Ocean acidification is a related effect of dissolved anthropogenic CO₂, chemically distinct from warming itself.
items.mitigation: Mitigation reduces greenhouse-gas emissions or increases their removal from the atmosphere. Examples include energy efficiency, low-carbon electricity and protection of carbon stores. Nuclear power is low-carbon but is not normally classified as renewable; evaluate each option by its full effects.

adaptation.rule: Adaptation is adjustment to actual or expected climate effects to reduce harm or use opportunities. Examples include flood protection, heat-health plans and changes to farming. It reduces vulnerability but does not necessarily reduce greenhouse-gas emissions; adaptation and mitigation address different parts of the problem.
examples: Floodable open space and drainage design can reduce damage during intense rainfall.

rates.title: Rates of Reaction
rates.intro: How fast a reaction goes — and the four factors that control it. Topic 6 in the teacher's revision booklet.

definition.title: What is rate?
definition.body: A reaction rate describes how quickly a measured amount of reactant decreases or product increases. Average rate = change in amount ÷ elapsed time; state the measured quantity and units. Concentration-based rates for different species are related by the equation's stoichiometric coefficients.

collision.title: Collision theory
collision.body: Collision theory models reactions as effective encounters between reacting particles. A productive collision requires sufficient energy to overcome an activation barrier and a suitable orientation. More collisions do not guarantee a faster reaction unless the frequency of successful encounters increases.

temperature.name: Temperature
temperature.rule: Raising temperature usually increases reaction rate because a larger fraction of particles can overcome the activation barrier. Collision frequency also changes. The size of the increase depends on the reaction and temperature range; a 10 °C rise does not universally double rate.
examples: Food in the fridge lasts longer (low T slows bacterial growth).
Cooking pasta in boiling water (100 °C) is faster than in warm water (50 °C).
temperature.tip: Activation-energy effect dominates over speed effect. Drawing a Maxwell–Boltzmann curve: more particles cross E_a at higher T.

concentration.name: Concentration (and pressure for gases)
concentration.rule: Increasing a reactant concentration often increases the frequency of encounters and hence reaction rate. For gases, increasing partial pressure at fixed temperature increases concentration. The quantitative dependence is determined experimentally; doubling concentration need not double rate.
examples: Dilute HCl reacts slowly with Mg; concentrated HCl reacts quickly.
Increasing pressure on gases (e.g., Haber process) acts like concentration.

surfaceArea.name: Surface area (of solids)
surfaceArea.rule: When a solid reacts at its surface, increasing its exposed area generally increases the total reaction rate. Dividing a fixed mass into smaller pieces exposes more contact area. This changes rate, not the amount of product possible from that mass alone.
examples: Powdered marble + HCl fizzes vigorously; a marble lump reacts slowly.
Flour explosions in mills — fine powder gives huge surface area and combusts rapidly.
surfaceArea.tip: Total mass is the same, but surface area can be 100×+ greater for fine powder.

catalyst.name: Catalyst
catalyst.rule: A catalyst increases reaction rate through an alternative mechanism with a lower effective activation barrier and is regenerated overall. It can take part in intermediate steps. It changes neither the reaction's enthalpy change nor the equilibrium composition at a fixed temperature.
examples: MnO₂ catalyses 2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂ (rapid bubbling).
Iron in the Haber process (N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃).
Enzymes in your body — biological catalysts (amylase, pepsin).
catalyst.tip: A catalyst may change a mechanism or product selectivity; for the same net reaction it does not change ΔH or equilibrium.

organic.title: Organic chemistry — intro
organic.body: Organic chemistry studies carbon compounds, especially their structures and reactions. Hydrocarbons contain only C and H. Acyclic alkanes have formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂; acyclic monoalkenes have CₙH₂ₙ. Alcohol and carboxylic-acid functional groups are –OH and –COOH; a formula alone may not identify a unique structure.

contrast.en: A classification is defined by structure or a specified process; similar-looking formulas need not have the same behaviour.
contrast.ru: Классификация опирается на строение или определённый процесс; сходные формулы не гарантируют одинакового поведения.

redox.title: Redox reactions
redox.body: Oxidation is electron loss and reduction is electron gain; they occur together in a redox reaction. More generally, oxidation raises oxidation state and reduction lowers it. A reducing agent is itself oxidised; an oxidising agent is reduced. Oxidation state is a bookkeeping quantity, not always an atom's actual charge.

contrast.en: Oxidation loses electrons or increases oxidation number; reduction gains electrons or decreases oxidation number. Oxygen is not required for every redox reaction.
contrast.ru: Окисление отдаёт электроны или повышает степень окисления; восстановление принимает электроны или понижает её. Не всякая ОВР требует кислорода.

electrochem.title: Electrochemistry
electrochem.body: Electrolysis uses electrical energy to drive a non-spontaneous redox reaction. Reduction occurs at the cathode and oxidation at the anode. In an electrolytic cell these are negative and positive respectively; signs reverse in a galvanic cell. Products depend on the electrolyte, electrodes and conditions.

contrast.en: Oxidation is always at the anode; reduction at the cathode. Their signs depend on whether the cell is galvanic or electrolytic.
contrast.ru: На аноде всегда идёт окисление, на катоде — восстановление. Знаки электродов зависят от того, гальванический элемент это или электролизёр.

Temperature: changes the energy distribution and the fraction of collisions able to react.

equilibrium.title: Dynamic equilibrium — intro
equilibrium.body: Dynamic equilibrium in a closed system occurs when forward and reverse reaction rates are equal, so macroscopic composition stays constant. Reactant and product concentrations need not be equal. Changes in conditions can shift equilibrium; a catalyst speeds approach to equilibrium without changing its composition at a fixed temperature.

contrast.en: At equilibrium the forward and reverse rates are equal; concentrations are constant but need not be equal. A catalyst changes the time to equilibrium, not its composition.
contrast.ru: При равновесии равны скорости прямой и обратной реакций; концентрации постоянны, но не обязаны быть равны. Катализатор меняет время установления равновесия, а не его состав.

atomicStructure.title: Atomic structure
atomicStructure.body: An atom has a small positively charged nucleus containing protons and usually neutrons, surrounded by electrons described by quantum states rather than fixed planetary orbits. Atomic number Z is proton count; mass number A is proton plus neutron count. A neutral atom has Z electrons.

contrast.en: Atomic number Z counts protons. Mass number A counts nucleons in one isotope; relative atomic mass is an isotopic average.

isotopes.title: Isotopes
isotopes.body: Isotopes are atoms of one element with the same proton count but different neutron counts, so they have the same Z and different A. Their electronic structures and chemical behaviour are usually very similar, but isotope mass can affect physical properties and reaction rates.

periodicTable.body: The periodic table orders elements by increasing atomic number. Periods are rows and IUPAC groups are columns numbered 1–18. reactions.title: Reactions & Equations
reactions.intro: Types of chemical reactions and how to balance equations correctly.

combination.name: Combination (synthesis)
combination.rule: A combination reaction forms a single product substance from two or more reactant substances. A schematic form is A + B → AB; an actual equation must use correct formulae and balanced coefficients. This classification can overlap with others, such as oxidation.
examples: 2H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2H₂O(l) — hydrogen burns in oxygen
CaO(s) + H₂O(l) → Ca(OH)₂(aq) — quicklime + water
N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) → 2NH₃(g) — Haber process
combination.tip: Reaction classification does not determine the sign of ΔH; consider the full energy balance.

contrast.en: Coefficients change numbers of particles; changing a formula’s subscripts changes the substance. Atoms and total charge must balance.
contrast.ru: Коэффициенты меняют числа частиц; изменение индексов формулы меняет вещество. Числа атомов и общий заряд должны сохраняться.

decomposition.name: Decomposition
decomposition.rule: A decomposition reaction converts one compound into two or more product substances. It may be driven by heat, light or electricity. For example, CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂ on heating; decomposition changes chemical identity rather than merely separating a mixture.
examples: 2H₂O₂(aq) → 2H₂O(l) + O₂(g) — peroxide with MnO₂ catalyst
CaCO₃(s) → CaO(s) + CO₂(g) — limestone heated
2H₂O(l) → 2H₂(g) + O₂(g) — electrolysis of water
decomposition.tip: Thermal decomposition of carbonates is a classic G9 example.

displacement.name: Single displacement
displacement.rule: A displacement reaction occurs when one element replaces another in a compound. For example, zinc reduces copper ions: Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu. Reactivity-series predictions apply under specified conditions; competing reactions and protective surface films can affect what is observed.
examples: Zn(s) + CuSO₄(aq) → ZnSO₄(aq) + Cu(s) — blue colour fades, brown copper deposits
Mg(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl₂(aq) + H₂(g) — magnesium 'fizzes'

doubleDisplacement.name: Double displacement (precipitation)
doubleDisplacement.rule: In a double-displacement reaction, ions exchange partners. A precipitation reaction is the case where dissolved ions form an insoluble solid, for example Ag⁺ + Cl⁻ → AgCl(s). Ion exchange does not always produce a precipitate; water or gas formation can also drive reactions.
examples: AgNO₃(aq) + NaCl(aq) → AgCl(s)↓ + NaNO₃(aq) — white precipitate of silver chloride
Pb(NO₃)₂(aq) + 2KI(aq) → PbI₂(s)↓ + 2KNO₃(aq) — bright yellow precipitate
doubleDisplacement.tip: Memorise common insoluble compounds: AgCl, BaSO₄, CaCO₃, PbI₂. They appear as the precipitate.

combustion.name: Combustion
combustion.rule: Combustion is an exothermic reaction of a fuel with an oxidant, usually oxygen in this course. Complete combustion of a hydrocarbon forms CO₂ and H₂O. Inadequate oxygen or mixing can cause incomplete combustion, producing CO and/or soot as well as other products.
examples: CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(g) — methane gas
2C₈H₁₈(l) + 25O₂(g) → 16CO₂(g) + 18H₂O(g) — petrol (octane)
combustion.watchOut: Complete combustion needs an adequate oxygen supply and effective mixing; flame colour alone is not a quantitative gas analysis.

neutralisation.name: Neutralisation
neutralisation.rule: Neutralisation is reaction between an acid and a base. For a strong acid and hydroxide alkali in dilute water, the net equation is H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l), with heat released. Other acid–base reactions can have different products; the final solution is not automatically pH 7.
examples: HCl(aq) + NaOH(aq) → NaCl(aq) + H₂O(l)
H₂SO₄(aq) + 2KOH(aq) → K₂SO₄(aq) + 2H₂O(l)
2HNO₃(aq) + Mg(OH)₂(s) → Mg(NO₃)₂(aq) + 2H₂O(l)
neutralisation.tip: H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O applies to strong aqueous acid with hydroxide alkali; weak acids require different ionic notation.

moles.title: The mole
moles.body: The mole is the SI unit of amount of substance. One mole contains exactly 6.02214076 × 10²³ specified entities, such as atoms, molecules or ions. Use n = m/M for a pure substance. Gas molar volume depends on temperature and pressure; it is not part of the mole's definition.

acidsBases.intro: pH scale, indicators, and key reactions of acids.

acid.name: Acid
acid.rule: In the Brønsted–Lowry model, an acid donates H⁺ to another species. In water, an acid increases hydronium, H₃O⁺, often written H⁺(aq). Acid strength describes the extent of ionisation in a given solvent; concentration describes how much acid is present per volume.
examples: HCl (hydrochloric acid) — stomach acid
H₂SO₄ (sulfuric acid) — car batteries
HNO₃ (nitric acid) — fertilisers
CH₃COOH (ethanoic / acetic acid) — vinegar (weak)
acid.tip: Strong acids fully ionise in water (HCl → H⁺ + Cl⁻). Weak acids only partly ionise (CH₃COOH ⇌ CH₃COO⁻ + H⁺).

contrast.en: Strength describes the extent of ionisation or reaction with water; concentration describes amount per volume. They are different quantities.

base.name: Base
base.rule: In the Brønsted–Lowry model, a base accepts H⁺. Hydroxide ions, carbonate ions and ammonia can act as bases. School classifications also call many metal oxides basic because they react with acids. A base need not be soluble and its reaction need not produce water.

MgO (magnesium oxide) — white powder
CaCO₃ (calcium carbonate) — chalk, limestone

alkali.name: Alkali
alkali.rule: An alkali is a water-soluble base that produces an alkaline aqueous solution with excess OH⁻ over H₃O⁺. Sodium hydroxide releases OH⁻ on dissolving; ammonia forms some OH⁻ by reacting with water. Thus an alkali need not contain hydroxide ions before dissolution.

Ca(OH)₂ (calcium hydroxide, limewater) — used to test for CO₂

salt.name: Salt
salt.rule: A salt is an ionic compound made of cations and anions in an electrically neutral ratio. In school inorganic chemistry, salts contain metal or ammonium cations and acid-residue anions. Neutralisation is one preparation method; salts can also form by other reactions and need not give neutral solutions.
examples: HCl + NaOH → NaCl (table salt) + H₂O
H₂SO₄ + Cu(OH)₂ → CuSO₄ (blue) + 2H₂O
HNO₃ + KOH → KNO₃ + H₂O
salt.tip: Name a salt: first word from the metal/base, second from the acid. HCl → chloride; H₂SO₄ → sulfate; HNO₃ → nitrate.

contrast.en: A salt is not necessarily neutral in water, and it need not be made by acid–alkali neutralisation.
contrast.ru: Раствор соли не обязательно нейтрален; соли получают не только нейтрализацией кислоты щёлочью.

litmus.name: Litmus
litmus.rule: Litmus is an acid–base indicator with different colours across a transition range: red in sufficiently acidic solution and blue in sufficiently alkaline solution, with intermediate colours between. It gives a broad classification, not a precise pH measurement.

reactions.title: Acid reactions — the FOUR you must memorise

metal.name: Acid + reactive metal → salt + hydrogen
metal.rule: Many metals above hydrogen in the reactivity series react with dilute non-oxidising acids to form a salt and H₂. For example, Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂. Oxidising acids, surface films and conditions can change the products or prevent an observable reaction.
examples: Zn(s) + 2HCl(aq) → ZnCl₂(aq) + H₂(g)
Mg(s) + H₂SO₄(aq) → MgSO₄(aq) + H₂(g)
2Al(s) + 6HCl(aq) → 2AlCl₃(aq) + 3H₂(g)
metal.watchOut: Reactive group 1 metals (Na, K) react EXPLOSIVELY with acid — never test these in school.

carbonate.tip: Acid rain attacks limestone buildings via this reaction — over decades, statues are eroded.

alkali.name: Acid + alkali → salt + water (neutralisation)
alkali.rule: An acid reacts with a hydroxide alkali to form salt and water. H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O is the net equation when both are fully dissociated. For weak acids or ammonia, keep the weakly ionised species in the ionic equation; equivalence does not always mean pH 7.
examples: HCl(aq) + NaOH(aq) → NaCl(aq) + H₂O(l)
H₂SO₄(aq) + 2NaOH(aq) → Na₂SO₄(aq) + 2H₂O(l)
HNO₃(aq) + KOH(aq) → KNO₃(aq) + H₂O(l)
alkali.tip: Dilute strong acid–hydroxide neutralisation releases roughly 57 kJ per mole of water; this value is not universal for every acid–base reaction.

energy.title: Energy Changes
energy.intro: Exothermic and endothermic reactions, energy diagrams, calculations.

items.exothermic: An exothermic reaction transfers heat from the reacting system to its surroundings. At constant pressure its enthalpy change is negative: ΔH = H(products) − H(reactants) < 0. The surroundings may warm; the reaction can still require an initial activation-energy input.
items.endothermic: An endothermic reaction absorbs heat from its surroundings. At constant pressure ΔH = H(products) − H(reactants) > 0. Products have higher enthalpy than reactants in the stated conditions. A temperature decrease can indicate heat absorption, but temperature and energy are different quantities.

exothermic.name: Exothermic reactions
exothermic.rule: An exothermic reaction transfers heat from the reacting system to its surroundings. At constant pressure its enthalpy change is negative: ΔH = H(products) − H(reactants) < 0. The surroundings may warm; the reaction can still require an initial activation-energy input.
examples: CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l): standard combustion enthalpy near 298 K is about −890 kJ per mole of methane.
Dilute strong acid + hydroxide: H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l), about −57 kJ per mole of water formed.
Respiration in your body: C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + ENERGY (powers life).
Hand warmers — iron oxidation: 4Fe + 3O₂ → 2Fe₂O₃ + heat. Activated by air.
Self-heating cans of coffee.
exothermic.tip: On an energy profile diagram: products LOWER than reactants. ΔH = E(products) − E(reactants) < 0.

contrast.en: Breaking bonds requires energy; making bonds releases it. Overall heat change depends on both contributions.
contrast.ru: Разрыв связей требует энергии, образование связей выделяет её. Общий тепловой эффект зависит от обоих вкладов.

Products have higher enthalpy than reactants in the stated conditions. A temperature decrease can indicate heat absorption, but temperature and energy are different quantities.

endothermic.watchOut: Photosynthesis requires light energy; absorbing radiation is not the same process as absorbing heat from surroundings.

profiles.body: An energy profile plots an energy measure against reaction progress. A one-peak curve is a simplified model.

calorimetry.title: Calorimetry
calorimetry.body: Calorimetry infers heat transfer from measured temperature change. For a solution, q(solution) ≈ mcΔT; if other heat transfers are negligible, q(reaction) ≈ −q(solution). At constant pressure, molar ΔH ≈ −mcΔT/(1000n) in kJ mol⁻¹ when c is in J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹.
